utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are very disappointed for the delay. Mr. Re, could you please tell us the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay in relation to the witness. There was some delay in relation to the e-court system before that. The witness sought some additional protective measures. There is some information I would like to provide to the Court, if we could go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this Bench believes that all these matters is triggered off by the protective measures. Here we believe it's necessary to remind both parties of the Rules, as well as the jurisprudence of this Tribunal for granting of the protective measures. Article 21 of the ICTY Statute stipulates that the Trial Chamber shall ensure that a trial is fair and expeditious with full respect for the rights of the accused and a due regard for its protection of victims and witnesses. There are five or six balancing tests which has been adopted before this Tribunal ever since the first case, that is, the Tadic case, to determine whether protective measures is to be granted to a witness; namely, first, there must be real fear for the safety of the witness or his family. Two, the evidence to be furnished by the witness must be sufficiently relevant and important to the Prosecution's case. Thirdly, there must be a lack of prima facie evidence that witness is untrustworthy. Fourthly, there must be a lack of a witness protection programme available. Fifth, any measure taken should be strictly necessary. The sixth, protective measures are to be granted only in exceptional circumstances and on a case-by-case basis. I believe that is a summary of the jurisprudence for granting of the protective measures for the witnesses before this Tribunal, and this criteria is applicable to the witnesses of both parties. Well, having said that, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Re, the witness is yours. Examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness F, I want to show you a piece of paper which has your name, date of birth, and place of birth on it. And when you get it, I want you to look at the piece of paper and tell me if it correctly records those details.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for one moment for some personal details, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness F, can you please briefly tell the Trial Chamber, as briefly as possible, what your duties were in your job in 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly did that -- did -- what exactly did that entail? What sort of things did you and your men do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: At the time, we had to formulate certain measures and rules concerning the manner of the protection of those facilities. That meant that in all facilities we had a reception desk or a reception service. Then, as I've already mentioned, we had to ensure protection in the residence, protection while in movement and protection in every other sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Protection of who? Who precisely were you protecting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It was necessary to protect the commander of the army at the time. That was General Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the deputies? Were -- was your department involved in the protection of the deputies, including Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: According to the rules of service and other rules of the security services, other generals, the chiefs of the administrations at the time and deputies of the commander or the Chief of Staff, did have a right to certain security protection measures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you, if you could please answer this as directly as you possible can: What protective measures, if any, did you provide for the deputies? That is, Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Siber and the other one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: We had security for them where they worked. We had a reception service at the facilities where they worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the reception service involve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: If anybody, whoever it was, wanted to reach those persons, those senior officers and so on, they had to pass through that check. They had to be announced. They had to go through the reception service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a registration, like a logbook or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did it record the names of people who visited the commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It was a rule. They had to be written down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred a moment ago to facility protection. What do you mean by "facility"? Are you talking about buildings, material, or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: These were the seats of commands, administrations or parts of the Main Staff. Since they were placed in several buildings or facilities, then -- these are the buildings or facilities that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these the facilities in Central Sarajevo, near the eternal flame, in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, mostly they were in the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was your office physically located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: My office was in the pre-war students residence hall, called Mladen Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Halilovic's office in that building or another one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic's office was perhaps 50 to 70 metres away from my building, but those two buildings were physically connected. However, they had different entrances and they were in the same street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Siber's office? Where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think that he was about 100 metres further down. I think that the name of that facility was Privredna Banka, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the commander, Rasim Delic's office, where was his office located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Commander Delic's office was located in a company building. The company was called Vranica. It was across the street from Mr. Halilovic's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your role also involve gathering -- you -- I withdraw that. A moment ago you mentioned information and data. Did your job involve the gathering of information and data on persons and organisations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'd -- I object -- I make it quite clear, I object to any leading on what this person's role was. Let him explain what his role was and let it not be suggested to him, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, I believe that you have to build up your case step by step. Maybe you could ask a general question first, and then go into the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned "information and data." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: This is the protection of the archive and archive documents, so that they would physically not be taken out of the headquarters of the commands. We also drafted rules and regulations and instructs on how to keep and preserve these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the role of your department involve any gathering of intelligence? And if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: My department could also work on the gathering of intelligence from various sources, from persons and other ways. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directed at what? What sort of intelligence would your department -- or did your department gather and why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: We were supposed to gather information -- all kinds of information which would have a negative effect or were directed against facilities or persons from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which individuals or groups were you interested in who had information which could have a negative effect or be directed against facilities or persons on the Main Staff? In other words, what were your targets?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'd object to that. He hasn't said he had any targets. My learned friend's question seems to me really to be what were his sources, and he can ask that question. But the witness hasn't said that he had targets. What he said is he gathered information to protect the people in the facilities of the Main Staff. So I object to the way that question was phrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can rephrase it. It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sources, targets, sources. What were your sources of information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It's like this: Every day we had meetings, morning meetings, reporting, briefings, and so on and so forth. Sometime in early 1993 we started to receive various kinds of information from subordinate units - for example, from the security service of the 1st Corps - and the state security. Besides that, some citizens also would come and report things in different ways about the inadequate activities of some members of two brigades which were part of the 1st Corps. These are the 9th Motorised and the 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you or your department interested in this particular information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It wasn't my department that was particularly interested, but it was my obligation to participate in these morning briefings, and I was told there to carry out adequate protection measures in relation to some intentions of those two brigades or, actually, some individuals from those two brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you just excuse me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that a little later, Witness F. I want to ask you at the moment about the physical protection of the commanders and deputy commanders. Specifically, just very briefly, what protection did you organise for the commander, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think that those measures at that time, physical protection measures, were something that the commander and the deputies claimed a right to. They didn't allow us to do that, even though they had physical protection units. They themselves in a way actually organised this protection. If it's necessary, I can provide examples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. But Mr. Halilovic, what -- what was his protection unit? Who was protecting him, and how was that organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: At the time, I must admit, was not so well informed about that area, although there were some guys there who were called the Delta Unit, I think. It consisted of some 30 guys who were there. We would see them often. They didn't have any particular contact with us, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to clarify your last answer. You said there were 30 guys and the Delta Unit and Mr. Halilovic. Can you just be more specific about what you saw and what you knew about his protection and the Delta Unit and these 30 people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think that at the time Mr. Halilovic had one man who was with him at all times. I don't know exactly what his name is. I've forgotten his name. But I did know him personally at that time. There were also one or two drivers with him too. The others were at the command. They were just there, present; although I don't know in what capacity, what they did, and so on. We were simply not absolutely informed about that particular manner of protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this Delta Unit from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It was there in Sarajevo. The information was quite restricted, so I really couldn't tell you -- I know that it was in Sarajevo, and I think that the name of its commander was Dino. That was his nickname or something like that. I don't know where their headquarters were, and I don't know how many of them there were, but I think that their role was of a combat nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your knowledge of their relationship to Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would object to this. I think we're talking about the Delta Unit here. And if my friend has a good reason for asking the questions, he should say what it is, because otherwise this looks entirely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I withdraw that question. I'll ask another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness F, the Delta Unit, which corps was it from? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No, I don't know. If I can just give a clarification. I think that later, in a certain period of the transformation of the army, it was transferred to the 1st Corps, but I really cannot remember the exact time period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little earlier you mentioned the 9th and the 10th Brigades in Sarajevo. Which corps were they a part of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the Army of the B and H then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware in 1993 of who Ramiz Delalic was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. I knew who he was, although I didn't communicate with him except for one occasion, during a one-day seminar which we organised at the headquarters of his brigade command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he, to your knowledge, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: He had a reputation, you could say, of being a person with a shady past and somebody who was known to police and official security organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you gain your information that he was a person known to have a shady past?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: We received the information from the State Security Service and also from citizens, friends, and so on, and actually this was something that was general knowledge around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "a shady past"? What was he alleged to have done in the past?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I can tell you that when I was taking a statement from him and during my conversation with him, he told me that he had spent several -- served several terms in prison, both in the country and also abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Probably because of criminal activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this an attack being made by the Prosecutor on the credibility of one of their own witnesses? Because if it is, it's wholly impermissible and improper. If it's relevant for some other reason, then it had better be spelled out, because Ramiz Delalic, as we understand it, is going to be called in this case by the Prosecutors, presumably as a witness of truth. So we -- that needs to be clarified right now, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But I believe that there will be a lot of questions concerning with this person later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can assure the Court that you're right, but the question is whether Mr. Re is to be permitted to lead evidence that's adverse about Ramiz Delalic in this way when he's going to call or at least somebody from the Prosecutor is going to call Mr. Delalic in person to give evidence either on videolink or here later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, the answer to that is quite easy: It's in the indictment, the pre-trial brief. We opened on it, that one of the planks of the Prosecution case is the accused's use of criminal elements within the 9th and 10th Brigades, and one of the persons -- or two people involved were Caco and Celo. And as Your Honour, and especially the Presiding Judge, Judge Liu, is aware in this Tribunal often witnesses are called who the Prosecution will submit should be believed on some things but not on others, and that may well be our ultimate submission with Mr. Delalic. I'm not attacking his credibility. I'm leading evidence as to the reputation of those particular brigades and that goes to the inquiry notice of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your last answer was probably -- "Probably because of criminal activities." Are you able to say now from memory what those criminal activities were that he told you about, if he did in fact tell you about them in the interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That was not the topic of our conversation, so I didn't ask him anything in particular about that, and he probably wouldn't tell me either. If we're talking about before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Look, just to clarify this last part. When did you interview him? And I'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I spoke to him on the 27th or the 28th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that -- I'll come back to this later. And was that part of Operation Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about a person called Musan Topalovic, Caco? Did you know of him in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you know of him in 1993? I'll make this clear. This is before -- before Operation Neretva.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of Musan Topalovic, Caco, probably in early 1993, probably from the point in time when he was appointed commander of that brigade, but I never actually saw him. He was a man who was acting from the background, if I can put it that way. He didn't like to be in the public eye. Most of the population in Sarajevo never saw him. He did not appear on television or the media and so on and so forth. I know that at that time they said that he was a very brave fighter and that his -- he enjoyed quite a reputation among his -- the people in his unit. He was quite respected. But after a while, we began to find out some things about his illegal activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come to that in a moment. I just want you to ask -- tell me briefly to which brigade was Ramiz Delalic attached and to which brigade was Musan Topalovic attached.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Ramiz Delalic was a commander of the 9th Motorised Brigade for a while and then later the deputy commander, while Musan Topalovic was the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade. I think it was the -- a mountain brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the military security service have an officer in the 1st Corps or in the 9th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: In the security services' structure, as part of the 1st Corps, I think that there was a security service department and then the brigades had a security service sector, and of course there were people working in these services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the relationship between military security service in the 9th Motorised Brigade and Mr. Delalic? This question is directed toward the quality of the relationship.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know enough about that, because the 9th Motorised Brigade was subordinated to the corps and all information which came from the security service of the 9th Brigade were sent to the 1st Corps and then the 1st Corps would then forward it to us. So I cannot really give you a specific answer. Although I do think that the relationship between Ramiz Delalic and his security service wasn't bad, and I can clarify that. In early 1993, I myself and the security administration service deputy -- commander and his deputy went to the brigade for a seminar. Our objective was in some way to introduce and instruct those people about the methodology of the work of those services, although the person who was in the security service of the 9th Motorised Brigade was a professional. I think that he had retired from the State Security Service. His name was Tomo Juric. He was a Croat by ethnicity. I think that he was a serious, mature man and that he was very well versed in the methodologies and principles of operation of those services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your awareness of Mr. Delalic's attitude towards the military security service, if you had any knowledge of his attitude and if he had an attitude towards the military security service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: At the seminar which we attended, we had been there for some time and then at some point Ramiz Delalic appeared. He was quite professional in his behaviour towards us. He didn't create any problems, although he did have an attitude toward some people from his own service, from the brigade. I could say that he had some problems because he had acquired some information -- actually, written information about him and his activities, and that is why we had actually gone there in the first place, in a way to ease the situation in that respect and avoid further problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to be precise. Well, what was the information? What was he supposed to have done that cause you to go there? As briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what it was all about, but I know that there were some information from the security service that had leaked, or as we say, this information was leaked, and in a way he ordered his people that they could not communicate with the security services unless it was through him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear he'd said about the security services and talking directly to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: He simply said that no one could go and communicate with members of the services without his knowledge. Something to that effect. Although I have to be honest and say that at that time his conduct towards us was very proper and professional and he did express a kind of wish for cooperation and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did your service get to know about his behaviour? That's Ramiz Delalic's.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Our service learned about his behaviour -- or at least, I can tell you about myself personally. I learned about that through morning meetings and briefings, through staff meetings. I learned the -- about the information received from the State Security Service and the security service of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've asked you about Ramiz Delalic. I want to ask you about the 9th Motorised Brigade. What was your information as to its reputation and behaviour in Sarajevo before Operation Neretva?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The 9th Motorised Brigade, at least based on what we know and the information that was available to me, was primarily within the composition of the 1st Corps. In addition to that, it was one of stronger brigades in terms of its composition, manning, and equipment. It held a very important position line in Sarajevo and had within its composition five battalions which were combat battalions defending that line. Naturally, they rotated, but they were positioned there. Within its composition, it also had one company which was a so-called assault company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber what you heard, if anything, about the behaviour of the assault company before Operation Neretva.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I, as a member of the security service, through daily briefings and staff meetings learned firsthand about the activities of all brigades within the BH army and especially those units, the 9th and the 10th Brigades, because they had engaged in unlawful activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those? What did you hear? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: As for the 9th Brigade, we received information that they in a way terrorised certain citizens by extorting money from them, seizing motor vehicles, property, and so on. I received that information mostly via the morning staff meetings and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mostly via the morning staff meetings. What other sources of information did you have apart from the morning staff briefings? Who else told you this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: We could also use other sources of information, meaning individuals, the media, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said you mostly got it from staff meetings. What I want you to tell the Trial Chamber is who else or how else did you hear specifically about the activities of -- these illegal activities of the 9th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: We received that information from our sister service, the security service -- State Security Service and the security service of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier, "As for the 9th Brigade, we received information." To which part of the 9th Brigade were you referring? All of it or part of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I've just told you that that brigade had five battalions which held the defence line. Within their composition, they had the so-called assault company. I don't know about the number of personnel in that unit. So that was the unit that in a way could have engaged in criminal activity. The other troops from other battalions I believe had nothing to do with those acts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the -- which unit was Ramiz Delalic in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Ramiz Delalic was initially commander and later deputy commander of the 9th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge, do you know, of the assault unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know. That information was in a way off limits to us. We didn't know about that. And I, in my position, did not know who was the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the illegal activities of the 10th? What were those and what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: At the time, I believe already early in 1993, we started receiving information, again from the security service of the 1st Corps and the State Security Service and also through the morning meetings and briefings and so on. That was the source of my information. In addition to that, citizens would come in, sometimes even our friends, and report about that activity. In actual fact, that was well known in Sarajevo that occasionally it would happen that people would be picked from the street and taken to the command of that brigade and later on taken to dig trenches in Sarajevo within the area of responsibility of the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell us a little bit more about the trench-digging you heard about. Who were the people taken there and what was the process of them being taken to the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: What I can remember now is that occasionally they would appear in a van in town and go to places where people assembled, mostly coffee bars, and they would then force young people, mostly men, to enter the van, take them to the command headquarters of the brigade, and there, based on what I knew at the time, they would be always met by Caco, Musan Topalovic, who would prescribe the number of days or the length of time during which they had to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the average period or time of service trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Sometimes it would be 10, 15 days, or longer. I don't know. I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these military people or civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know for a fact. Sometimes they would be soldiers. However, I think that these people were mostly civilians. They would select people right there in the street. They would ask the person to produce a military booklet, and if the person didn't have it, he would definitely be selected; if the person had by chance a military booklet on him showing that he belonged to a certain unit, then sometimes they would spare him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were these trenches that people were being taken to dig?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That was in the area of responsibility of the 10th Mountain Brigade on the left bank of Miljacka and on the slopes of the Trebevic Mount.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that in relation to the front line, to the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think it was across from the Serb positions. Those were the first front lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you say about the safety or danger to the civilians digging trenches in those front-line positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I wasn't there. I didn't see the situation. But if they were in front-line positions, that meant that there was always a possibility of them getting killed. That means that they were very exposed to danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from where in Sarajevo were the soldiers from the 10th taking civilians? Where were they finding them? Was there a particular area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think that was in the old part of the town, the so-called Stari Grad municipality. This is where they were mostly active. They defined that by themselves as their area of responsibility, which I believe was normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've -- you've just described hearing about people being taken from the streets to Caco's command and then taken to the front line to dig trenches. Did you yourself have any -- what was your attitude -- your own attitude, living in Sarajevo in 1993, to going into that area which was controlled by Caco's men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I lived right there. Let's say between the Stari Grad and Centar municipalities. I didn't volunteer to go to that area of responsibility there myself because it wasn't popular to go to that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean "it wasn't popular to go to that area"? Just elaborate on that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Because we from the security service believed that we could be possible targets and could be selected to go dig trenches, just like many others were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Trial Chamber about something that happened in July 1993 involving the 9th and 10th -- sorry, involving soldiers in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think that that happened sometime in early July. It was the 2nd or the 3rd of July. In the morning, at that time I, as usual, was in the headquarters of the military security service, and what happened was that part of the town which in a way belonged to those brigades, the 9th and the 10th, was suddenly blocked, blocked by the members of these two brigades. For example, I at the military security service in the morning was informed during our briefing - although there was quite a commotion and people were concerned - but we received information that the -- the operations centre facility was blocked, or the command and control centre of the BH army, which was housed in this so-called SDK building near the eternal flame. The building was blocked by the members of the 9th Motorised Brigade. The other part that was blocked was the part around -- where Commander Delalic [as interpreted] was. I think the street is called Kulovica [Realtime transcript read in error: "Kuce"] Street. And there's a bridge leading to that area. I can't remember what it was called now. What they did was they placed the metal hedgehogs, the so-called hedgehogs with barbed wire so that people couldn't pass. This was done by members of the 10th Brigade. In addition to that, we received information that the MUP was blocked, namely, the Stari Grad police station, as well as part of the Main Staff which was housed in the Faculty of Political Sciences. That building was blocked by the members of the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just stop you there for a second. The transcript said you said Commander Delalic. Did you say "Delalic" or Delic"? The street -- Kuce Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I said "Delic." What I wanted to say is that they blocked the street leading to the seat or the office of the army commander, Rasim Delic. I think that that was done by the members of the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, earlier in your testimony you told the Trial Chamber that your department was responsible for facility protection, and you've named the various Supreme Command facilities that your department was protecting. Did you have people in position of -- at those buildings on the day when the 9th and 10th blockaded that part of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, we did have our people there but not in position. I don't think we could use that term. These people were performing their regular duties at the reception desk and guarding whomever they were supposed to guard. When you say "position," for us that means something else. It -- it pertains to combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe that was inelegantly phrased. I meant going about their normal daily business. What happened to them during the blockading of these buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: They were disarmed on that occasion and taken away from those buildings. Later on we learned that their weapons had been taken away from them, in most cases their uniforms as well. They were humiliated, and returned to us after several days -- or perhaps on the same day. All of these events unfolded very quickly, so I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they taken to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: They were taken most likely to the headquarters of those brigades, the 9th and the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this blockade go on for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think it lasted one day, as far as I can remember now. Later on an agreement was reached - at least, that's what I heard - and the blockade was lifted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how did it come -- how did the blockade come to be lifted? Who was the agreement reached between? Who was involved in reaching the agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: What I learnt, since I was in the headquarters of the military security service administration, was that somebody from the command intervened with Mr. Halilovic and asked him to contact Ramiz Delalic and do something about it, and afterwards the blockade was lifted. This is what I remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just -- just so we can get the sequence. When did you learn that someone had asked Mr. Halilovic to contact Ramiz Delalic? Was it during the blockade or at a different time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: During the blockade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long after you learned that Mr. Halilovic had been asked to contact Mr. Delalic was the blockade ended or lifted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I think that it was lifted on the same day or very shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was -- what were you told was the reason for asking Mr. Halilovic to speak to Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Most likely they knew that -- they had some personal contacts, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your information working in military security service in 19 -- in July 1993 about the personal contact between Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: At the time, we -- or rather, I personally learned at the meetings, briefings, and so on that Mr. Halilovic was in permanent contact with Ramiz Delalic and Musan Topalovic. We learned that through the information that reached us. I received it firsthand. What I mean by that is that the information was not shown to me, but I learned about it during briefings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What action, if any, was taken against those members of the 9th and 10th Brigades who blockaded the Supreme Command headquarters on about the 2nd or 3rd of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: At the time, I think that nothing was done, no particular measures, because practically it was impossible. The reason for is that is that the Main Staff did not have any combat units at its disposal. It had no resources and no means to do anything about that. Those forces were outside of the command control and -- command and control of the 1st Corps and the army at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "those forces" -- my question was the 9th and the 10th. Is that who you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: At the time, we were unable to reach these people. In addition to that, we had a problem and we were hindered by the fact that we did not have sufficient information about their illegal activities. That means that we continued our intelligence work on verifying and proving their activities. Furthermore, we had information that they were in permanent contact with the Chief of Staff, Mr. Halilovic, and that in a way made any action of ours more difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your understanding of the reason why they were in permanent contact with Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. They were always under some kind of a pressure as though something was being prepared against them and there was something looming over them. As far as I know, that wasn't the case. Attempts were made to return these people under the command and control system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did their contact or their permanent contact with Mr. Halilovic make any action on your part more difficult?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Well, after all, Mr. Halilovic was the second highest ranking person in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't think that anything could be done without his consent -- or rather, nothing could be done against those brigades. I think that at the time there were attempts to contact Mr. Halilovic. I remember, for example, when somebody intervened to have a member of security service released, a member who was imprisoned by Musan Topalovic. Those attempts were made by the chief of the administration, and I don't know whether that was successful, whether the man was released. That means that they were on good terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you said it was your view that those forces, meaning the 9th and the 10th, were outside the command and control of the 1st Corps and the army at the time, meaning July 1993. Under whose command and control were the 9th and the 10th at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, he hasn't said they were under anyone's command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they were under any -- sorry. Were they, to your knowledge, under the command and control of any person or unit at the time? And if so, who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I can make a logical conclusion. If these two brigades blocked the Supreme Command -- or rather, not the Supreme Command but the Main Staff of the army and block their entire work, and if they're allowed to take away a member of the security service of their superior command, and at that time they also arrested the son of the army commander, they mistreated him, humiliated him, just like the member of the security service, then based on that it is logical to conclude that they were outside of the system. In addition to that, after some time a meeting was held at the level of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina during which a position was taken along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that an appropriate time? I think that's an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you prefer, we'll have a longer break you know. We'll resume at ten minutes after 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before the break, Witness F, you told the Trial Chamber that -- I'll just take you to your last answer, and it was about the knowledge of whether they were within the command and control of the army or the 1st Corps, and you said, "It was logical to conclude that they were outside of the system," and, in addition to that, "a meeting was held at the level of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina during which a position was taken along those lines." I just want to take you back to the first part of your answer, where you said "it was logical to conclude that they were outside of the system," that is, the system of the ABiH. To your knowledge, who were the 9th and 10th Brigades accountable to or who, if anyone, were they taking orders from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I can't say whether that was true or not, and I don't know who they received their orders from, but the things that the military security administration had at its disposal and then I myself, through meetings, documents, and so on, was that they were frequently directly in contact with the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what -- what was the significance in military terms of the 9th and -- the leaders of the 9th and 10th Brigades being in contact with Mr. Halilovic, the Chief of Staff? What was the significance from an intelligence perspective?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you -- you'd heard through meetings and documents that they were frequently directly in contact with the Chief of Staff, and you said that you had been led to conclude that they were outside of -- the army system. What's the significance in the context of that answer of them being outside the control of the army but in contact with the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Well, you can conclude that that wasn't logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why not? I mean, what do you mean by "not logical"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff, as the person number two of the B and H army, directly contacted the commanders of the brigades which were linked in the organisational sense to the 1st Corps. So I think that it wasn't logical to have such direct communication in that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why wasn't that logical, in your understanding of the way the ABiH worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: According to the command and control system, the brigades were linked to the corps and not to the Chief of Staff or the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you referring to the period before or after the blockade in July 1993 or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period approximately when we began to find out about this inadequate conduct of the people from those two brigades and, of course, after that key date between the 2nd and 3rd of July. I think that after that, it would have been logical not to have contacts directly with those people. This applies to the commander according to the rules and principles of command and control, because they were actually linked to the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to tell the Trial Chamber briefly about the meeting at the Presidency level in connection with the -- the 9th and the 10th Brigades. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise answer, but at the time the information that reached me during those briefings and at meetings, we were told, or it was said that at the level of the Presidency - I don't know who was presiding over it; I think it was probably Professor Dr. Pejanovic, who was the president of that commission for the protection of constitutional order, or something like that - at that meeting, Commander Rasim Delic expressed his views, and then after that probably the position was taken. That's what was said to us. But I wasn't present at that meeting, so I wasn't really directly interested in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any directions given to your department as a result of that meeting? Were you told to do anything arising from that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: After that period, immediately after the 3rd of July, we took a more offensive position or stance. Like it's called in the service, to gather more intelligence and to look at more incriminating actions, and we already had some indications that these activities of theirs would no longer be tolerated and that at some point measures would be taken to stop this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to tie your answer to the question. I was asking you about the meeting at the Presidency level. Were -- by your answer, do you mean that as a result of that meeting your section was directed to gather -- or the service was directed to gather more intelligence and look at the activities of those units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether it was because of that, whether we received some written document or not, but we had meetings constantly. Every morning we had a briefing where we would submit reports on our work. And after that, we would receive the directives and tasks for the forthcoming period, for the following days. This was not a particular task issued to my department. It was an overall -- a general task at the security service level that we all had to focus more on this problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was action taken against the 9th and the 10th at any point? I just want a very brief answer. And if so, when? And I'll come to what happened later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think on the 26th of October, 1993, that's when it was, following a political and military - when I say "military," I am thinking of the commander - so it was decided at that level that these activities of those two brigades should be stopped. There should be an end to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To clarify what you're saying, are you saying that it was after the 3rd of July incident that a decision was made at a higher level that their activities had to be stopped, directions were given to the intelligence services and so on to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just after the time frame. What happened in very brief -- in very brief terms between July and October? If you could just very briefly in general say what action was taken against the 9th and the 10th between July and October.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Between July and October, I think that nothing was done, except for the fact that the security service was active on the gathering of data and in a way was trying to prove that this activity was going on in order that the political structures and the military leadership would see what was really going on and that they would then make a decision to put an end to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier before the break the -- something that happened to Commander Delic's son. I want you to tell the Trial Chamber what you know of what happened and what your involvement in it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I cannot give you the specific time, but this was the period when things became critical, in July. This was when they began to arrest people from the army, specifically from the Main Staff and from the corps. For example, I know that a member of ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just complete that sentence, "I know that a member of ..."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That on that occasion a security -- a member of the security of the army commander was arrested. His son -- actually, his escort or the person who was a member of his personal security, that's -- that's who that person was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to go back to something. You said, "This was when they began to arrest people from the army ..." Now, in giving your evidence, would you -- if you're going to say "they," could you please help us by saying who "they" is every time you say "they." In the specific context of this answer, who is "they"? Who is "they" who began arresting people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think that this was done by members of the 10th Brigade. On this occasion, I would like the clarify one thing. I don't know that members of the 9th Brigade arrested anyone and in that way took people away and harassed them and abused them by making them dig trenches. This is something that was done by the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You specifically mentioned someone from the -- the son -- of a person who was a member of the personal security of the commander. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It was Admir or Almir Delic, something like that. He was a young man in his 20s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: He was taken to the command of Musan Topalovic, Caco, to the 10th Brigade. He was up there for a few days. The information that we had indicated that he was beaten up there, humiliated, abused, and so on and so forth, to such an extent -- he was humiliated to such an extent that he had to escape, risking his life, and he jumped from a wall from this command of the 10th Brigade to the headquarters of the UNPROFOR at that time. I think it was the Egyptian Battalion at the time, because the 10th Brigade was located right next to the Egyptian UNPROFOR battalion, and that's how he saved himself. He escaped, and they pulled him out and then sent him back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a statement taken from him as to what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I personally took his statement. I cannot recall all the particulars. It was a long time ago. All I know is that I personally took his statement and that statement has to be somewhere in the archives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what stands out from that statement about what they did to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Look, Your Honours, I haven't -- I haven't objected up to now, but this is becoming extremely remote. The witness took a statement from another person, who, as I understand, is not a witness in this case, about terrible things that happened to him at the 10th Brigade. I cast no aspersions on the witness's evidence. He's just responding, as he's entitled to do, to questions. But I submit this has gone too far in terms of speculative questioning. And asking for details of a statement from someone who is not being called, who was mistreated in a private place, captured by the 10th Brigade, is in my submission, just too remote from the trial of the man whose in prison, Sefer Halilovic. So I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think you have to remember that the hearsay evidence is admissible. Of course this piece of the evidence is a little bit remote, as you put it, but this witness took the statement of that person, and that issue is somehow relevant to our case and later on maybe we could see more relevance. So I will allow --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- Mr. Re to proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness F, do you remember -- the question was: What stands out from the statement that you took from Mr. Delic's son as to what the members of the 10th Brigade did to him when he was in captivity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I cannot remember right now, but I know that he was humiliated and abused. There's probably some information about that, but I know that it was said that this was so, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he managed to escape by leaping off a wall into an UNPROFOR base. Were you aware of any other efforts, apart from his own, being made to secure his release?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think that there were some direct interventions addressed to Musan Topalovic by some officers, but they were not successful. I think that one of our senior officers intervened directly by contacting Musan Topalovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said earlier that your understanding was that Mr. Halilovic was in constant contact with Musan Topalovic and Ramiz Delalic. Were you aware whether Mr. Halilovic ever intervened or was asked to in relation to Mr. Delic's son's release?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Halilovic was asked to intervene on behalf of Mr. Delic's son, but I know that this intervention was sought in relation to Amir Deljkic, who was a security service officer in the 1st Corps. I don't know what the outcome of that intervention was. I -- I don't know actually what happened later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what happened to Mr. Deljkic and when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Again, in this time of crisis, members of the 10th Brigade arrested Amir Deljkic. He was one of the chiefs of a part of the security service in the 1st Corps. He lived in the area of responsibility of the 10th Brigade and probably as he was passing there on his way to work or perhaps they knew where he lived - I don't know - on one occasion they intercepted him, arrested him, and took him to the command of the 10th Brigade. I also know that he was humiliated, abused, and really exposed to the basest forms of human behaviour. As far as I know, the chief of the security service administration intervened on his behalf by contacting Mr. Halilovic because we had information that his life was in danger. That's what we were told at the security administration, and I don't know what happened. I don't know if this intervention was successful or not. I must admit that I really didn't follow that situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're referring to Mr. Jasarevic there, when you said chief of the military security administration?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move to another area now; namely, Operation Neretva. When did you become aware of the name of an operation called Neretva?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I was told -- or actually, I knew by early September, again through those morning briefings where task were assigned and so on, that something was being prepared in the area of Herzegovina. I don't know exactly when I found out that the name of it was "Neretva." I don't know whether it was before the operation was carried out or after that, but I know that in some way we were told that some activities were being prepared on a larger scale in the territory of Herzegovina in early September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: In the Neretva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you told, if anything, was the aim of this particular operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I have to clarify one thing here, because I was not involved in combat activities and I was not entrusted with -- or had anything to do with the people or security services of the corps, so I really wasn't all that interested in details, so I didn't know what the objective was. But you could conclude that for yourself. Mostar was blockaded at the time, that whole area there, so it was quite normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told who, if anyone, was to be in charge of this particular operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I object to that. Your Honours, what he said - and this is at line 43 -- page 43, line -- lines 4 onwards - but what he said -- what the witness said was he "knew by early September, again through the morning briefings where the tasks were assigned and so on, that something was being prepared in the area of Herzegovina ... I don't know whether it was before the operation was carried out or after that, but I know it was in some way we were told that some activities were being prepared on a larger scale."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a minute. I want it to be clear what I'm objecting to fist. I'm objecting to him putting in the witness's mouth the term "operation" when the witness has simply said he knew about activities and some -- well, I won't repeat it, but what I've -- what I've read out there. So that's the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As I said, I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness F, in relation to those activities that you heard were about to be carried out in Herzegovina, were you told who, if anyone, was to be in charge of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: We heard at that time and we were told that the leader of those activities will be the Chief of Staff, Sefer Halilovic. This is what -- the information that I had at that time. This was unconfirmed information. I didn't see any paper to that effect or any particulars. I wasn't really informed about the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that information consistent or inconsistent with your understanding of Mr. Halilovic's role as the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, that question should be clarified. Does he mean the role of Mr. Halilovic's -- does he mean Mr. Halilovic's role as Chief of Staff generally speaking, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, if that's the case, that should be made clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally. Mr. Halilovic's duties generally as Chief of Staff. That is, what he did every day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know what he did every day. He was my superior officer in a way. In any case, the place and the role of the Chief of Staff of the army is something that would mean that in a way he was in charge or in command and control of a combat in the field, in charge of combat operations, directly or indirectly. It's something that I cannot say specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. My question was: Was the information that Mr. Halilovic was to be in charge of those activities consistent or inconsistent with your understanding of his general role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Well, it could be logical, but I didn't see a document or anything where this would be stated explicitly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know someone called Namik Dzankovic in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any connection with these activities in Herzegovina? And if so, what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Namik Dzankovic was a member of the security service administration at the time and also prior to that. I couldn't tell you the exact time period, but he left for family reasons and went to Herzegovina, to the area near Mostar. I know that during one of those morning briefings it was decided that in view of the fact that he was in that area, he should join that team. I think that the team was known as some kind of an inspection team under the leadership of the Chief of Staff and he was to join that team immediately. I think that he did join the team and performed duties from his scope of competence. Now, the question is as to what extent he was able to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Concerning the extent? To which extent? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Namik Dzankovic worked in the military security administration perhaps one year before that, as far as I know. I think that he's an educated man, an economist or an engineer by profession. I'm not sure. As far as I know, he had no prior work experience in the military services -- security services, and I think that in terms of professional competency he wasn't quite up to it. And even if he was, it would have been difficult to undertake all measures that his position would entail in that area. Simply speaking, within his operative competencies he had units or parts of units that were not familiar to him. I don't know whether he had security officers within those units. I don't know whether he received any instructions concerning that. And therefore, I think it was very difficult for him to put in place security protection measures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness F, did you yourself ever hear about civilians being killed at Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and how did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I can't say precisely the date, but I know for a fact that upon the return of these units from Herzegovina there was a lot of talk, even public talk, about something terrible having happened in the valley of the Neretva River or, rather, in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which units are you referring to returning from Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think that that involved part of the 10th Mountain Brigade, part of the 9th Motorised Brigade, and the so-called 2nd Independent Battalion. I'm not sure about its strength, but some parts of that battalion had been in that area as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about how the 10th and the 9th and the 2nd Independent Battalion came to be in Herzegovina or why they were there? What did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I am not familiar the information concerning who engaged those brigades, but again, based on the information we received in our daily morning briefings, they in a way either directly or indirectly had been selected by the Chief of Staff, Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In general terms, what was the reaction of the military security service and the authorities in relation to Grabovica, what had happened there, upon the return from Herzegovina of those three units you referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Upon the return of these units from Herzegovina, it was already decided that such activity would not be tolerated in the future and that serious measures have to be taken to prevent that. I know that an urgent plan was adopted at the highest level with involvement of certain police establishment to put an end to such activity and also to investigate the events in Grabovica. I know that the then-chief of military security administration had full-scale correspondence and this was reported to us at the daily briefings, that written instructions, directions, and so on had been sent to Herzegovina to Namik Dzankovic personally and also to the 6th Corps, I believe. In addition to that, I know that General Delic or the army commander established a commission. I'm not sure if it was called a commission, but at any rate it was a team set up to investigate the events, to identify the perpetrators, to conduct interviews, prepare evidence, and punish the perpetrators properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did what happened in Grabovica have any effect on the existing investigations into the activities of the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I did not understand your question entirely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier in your evidence that as from July 1993 a decision had been made to put an end to the activities of the 9th and the 10th. I'm taking you to Grabovica and when they returned. Did what happened in Grabovica have any effect on what was already occurring in relation to their activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think that that crime which had been perpetrated was the last straw and that it in fact just stepped up this intention to put an end to those activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And briefly, I want you to describe what happened in relation to the 9th and the 10th between their return from Herzegovina and Operation Trebevic, which I think you said was October the 26th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: On the 26th of October, 1993, according to the plan which had already been approved and signed both by political, military, and MUP officials, those activities were to be stopped. I know that it was planned to carry out an operation in the morning hours. Certain MUP intervention forces were engaged, an intervention unit, a battalion of military police with the Main Staff, and some other units which I cannot remember now, but at any rate they were from the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to pause there. I'll come to that in a moment. I'll ask you in a moment what happened between their return from Herzegovina and Operation Trebevic on the 26th of October. How was it planned? What happened? And what was your involvement? As briefly as you possibly can tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The work, the operative work, was intensified as well as gathering documents and information in order to be as prepared as possible when embarking on this operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what was your specific role in Operation Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: My specific role in Operation Trebevic was in the first place to conduct the initial triage or selection among the people from that brigade who had already been arrested. As regards those concerning whom we had no knowledge of their prior criminal activity, they were to be released and they were to go back to their regular daily tasks. As for those about whose criminal and other activities we had information, those people were taken into custody and sent to the central prison in order to be further processed, questioned, and so on. There were four to five hundred arrested persons who had gone through that initial triage or selection, which was not conducted by myself only. There was colleagues of mine working on that too. The final number of those taken into custody was about 50, and their activities were further investigated and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I jumped the gun a little bit. What I should have asked you before was - when I stopped you - you said that MUP, an intervention unit, a battalion of military police, and some other units from -- you think from the 1st Corps were engaged. Were they the units that arrested those four to five hundred people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think there was a mistake. Not from the 1st Corps. No. This military police battalion was from the Main Staff. However, that doesn't mean that people from the 1st Corps did not participate as well, because there were several units, and I don't know all the details concerning them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From which units were the people arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The people arrested were from the 9th and 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The final number, you said, taken into custody was about 50 and they were investigated. Did you interview any of those taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Correction: I said it was roughly 50. I don't know the exact number. That means that there could have been 40 and there also could have been 60 of them. I did not conduct interviews with them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness -- could the witness repeat the last question -- the last sentence. It was unclear to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took a statement and conducted an interview with Ramiz Delalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about those who were arrested but not taken into custody? What happened to them, the several hundred who weren't -- who weren't detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The people who were not taken into custody were immediately released. They went back to their units and their regular tasks. Our defence lines at that time and also always were exposed to great danger, were under attack from the enemy. And people had to go back to their daily tasks. There was no reason for us to hold them back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was a decision made that these people should be sent back and others kept in custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: In our daily meetings, briefings, and so on, it was said -- or rather, the position was taken at the level of the security service administration chief when he assembled all of us senior staff that we had to conduct ourselves professionally and properly at all times, and in case of persons concerning whom no information existed about their prior criminal activity, we had to release them to enable them to go back to their regular tasks. As for the other category of people concerning whom we had knowledge of their prior criminal or any other activity, we were to detain them, to investigate them further, and these people in fact were punished and served sentences for their prior activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you took a statement and conducted an interview with Mr. Delalic. Over how many days did you interview Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think it lasted seven to eight days. Perhaps even longer. About ten days. That's how long we interviewed him. On a daily basis, from the day he was arrested onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just -- I just want the place where it occurred. Where did you interview him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: We interviewed him in my then-office at the headquarters of the military service administration on the second floor of the hotel where we were housed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you very briefly list the topics that you interviewed him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object to this. This is just an attempt to get the statements of Mr. Delalic before the Court. He's coming. There's all sorts of reasons why it shouldn't be allowed. The primary one is that it's just statements from the witness. There can be no evidentiary value to this at all. And it's particularly to be objected to on a second basis, that he's coming. It may be that questions are asked of him arising from statements, but it may well be that there are no such questions. And the principle of oral evidence is a very important one at this Tribunal and shouldn't be undermined by this. So I object to this attempt to lead the substance on the topics of the statements by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the Prosecutor just asked a preliminary question, that is, the topic of the interview with Delalic. Of course Mr. Delalic will come here to give his testimony at a later stage, and that piece of the evidence may be served as part of the evidence for the purpose of the credibility of this witness or with Mr. Delalic. We are not going into the specific issues of his statement at this stage, but here it is just a topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's really the specific issues that I'm concerned with. I agree that I've risen at an early stage. It's in order that I don't jump up in the middle and interrupt the witness when he's given a bona fide answer. I agree with what Your Honour says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just the topics, please. No details. If you could just list them like they're under each other.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I will as far as I can remember, because I never saw that statement again. After I took the statement, I forwarded it to the department, which put it all together and forwarded it to the prosecutor's office. However, I can remember the topics. One of the topics was the crime in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The next one? The next one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The next one involved other incriminating acts concerning the 9th Motorised Brigade and the events in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The opinion of Delalic himself concerning all of that. The next topic was his attitude -- or rather, his relationship with the Chief of Staff, Sefer Halilovic. I cannot remember all the details, but the statements are there. There should be six or seven statements. I'm not sure about the exact number.
