All of them were signed by Ramiz Delalic, and perhaps you could acquire them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you about what had happened in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I anticipate the objection, and can I respond to the objection my learned friend has already made before? I know what the objection is, and if I can respond to it, it might be quicker to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, you may respond to the previous objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. The Prosecution wishes to lead evidence on this witness on two particular points: Firstly, Ramiz Delalic, what he told the investigating person - namely, Witness F - contemporaneously - that's on October the 26th or thereabouts, 1993 - about, firstly, Grabovica, what happened there; and, secondly, his relationship with the accused, Sefer Halilovic. It's probative and relevant for these particular reasons: First -- I mean, of course it's hearsay. But firstly, it's contemporaneous. And secondly, it's corroborative of anything that Ramiz Delalic himself might say in this -- before this Trial Chamber. So it's corroborative and, hence, probative, and, hence, relevant to the matters for determination by the Trial Chamber. And thirdly, if, for example, Ramiz Delalic did not come, even though he's on the list, for whatever reason, the evidence would be here. The Court can give it whatever weight it wishes, it being hearsay evidence, of what Ramiz Delalic said at the time had happened in Grabovica and his relationship with Sefer -- Sefer Halilovic, because the best evidence is, of course, the most contemporaneous evidence, as opposed to evidence given many years later. So, Your Honour, that's the basis upon which I wish to lead that evidence from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The best evidence is the evidence given in this court by the witness. My friend has just -- and I mean, no prosecutor could fail to know that, that that submission there is just mist and snow. The best evidence is the evidence to be given by Mr. Delalic. Your Honours, let me put something as -- what the Defence opinion is to assist the Court. They're not going to call Ramiz Delalic. A letter was sent to them yesterday asking them for their position on this. My learned friend has indicated now that one of his reasons for this question is that in case Mr. Ramiz Delalic doesn't come. Now, it's the Defence prediction that he won't come. And we are very concerned therefore about this and we think that -- that this is just an attempt to get these statements into evidence because it's -- assists the Prosecution case. But it can't be allowed. Firstly, it's not the best evidence. At this moment, Delalic is on the list. He's -- they say he's being called. So we must act on that basis. And if he is being called, then his is the best evidence. Therefore, these statements shouldn't be allowed in on that basis. Secondly, my learned friend says that this evidence would be corroborative of Mr. Delalic. And the answer to that is that really depends upon whether or not Mr. Delalic says now the same things that he said then. And then another question would arise as to whether indeed it is corroborative in any event. But you can't say it will be corroborative until that witness makes an appearance, and therefore it's too early for that -- that claim to be made. And -- just looking at -- could Your Honours just excuse me a moment. I want to respond to something else. Well, really the first point -- my friend made three points. He said it was contemporaneous. Well, it's not really contemporaneous. It's weeks later on the events of Grabovica. But that's an argument for another time. The second point is that one about -- about it being corroborative. Well, I've made my point about that. And the third one is that, as you'll see, my learned friend says, "If for example Ramiz Delalic did not come." Perhaps my friend can enlighten the Chamber as to why he thinks he might not come, and whether that's a decision that has already been made, or whether there is something about that in the atmosphere that we should all know about, bearing in mind that he's a witness that the Defence would have to and is currently investing a lot of time in preparing for. But all of those reasons pale into insignificance beside the main one, that at the moment he's a witness, he's coming, let him give his evidence. And in fact I submit that there should be no question of this -- of this proceeding. And in fact I think at the start of my objection to the last one my learned friend said as much. He said he just wanted the topics. And Your Honour allowed him to proceed at that time. And we've had a massive 180-change of direction at that stage. So in short, I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just in relation to the last point my learned friend raised about whether or not Ramiz Delalic is coming, he's on our list. As far as we are concerned, he is coming. I just said it for abundant caution. Often witnesses are on a list and for some reason they may not appear. That's all. Our intention at the moment is to call Ramiz Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that gives me great relief to hear that, because I believe that the witness list has been approved by the Trial Chamber and we are prepared to hear that witness in the future. I don't know when, but we are prepared for that. As for the evidence on that point, I agree with the Defence team; that is, that live witness testimony in this courtroom is the best evidence. Here this witness is trying to help us. But anyway, that is the secondhand hearsay evidence. So long we have the best evidence available in the future on the substantial issues in our view, we'll rely on that testimony in the future. So, Mr. Re, your question to this witness is not allowed at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness F, I wish to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can Exhibit P216 please be put on the screen. Before it's done, perhaps we could go into private session because it -- for this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Morrissey, are you ready for the cross-examination or you need more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the circumstances, I can commence, and the witness won't finish today, unfortunately. I'm in the Court's hands. And there are some questions. I can proceed with the witness now and not waste the Court's time. So I do have some matters I'm going to need to pursue. On the one hand, I won't waste time now; on the other hand, if we leave it all until tomorrow, it might take shorter. So I'm in the Court's hands. I'm ready to commence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since we still have 25 minutes to go, you may start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will. Cross-examined by Mr. Morrissey:

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, would you please redact that. I note I've committed the sin already once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was in that capacity that you extended -- you attended the daily briefing sessions which you've given evidence about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this Tribunal, we've heard of a -- a concept called "operative information" and that was explained to us by a witness named Mr. Jasarevic. Now, was the information that was used at those daily meetings operative information? Is that an accurate term to use in dealing with it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Sometimes we would use these -- this information acquired by operative means, but also we would use the information received from the SDB of the MUP, as well as the information of the security service of the 1st Corps. It was more -- probably more reliable information in the second instance. Operatively acquired information was less reliable. You would need to put in additional work to double-check it, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's the topic I wanted to ask you about. Where you received information from the State Security Services, you -- I take it you acted on the basis that they had already checked that information and assessed its reliability; is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The level of the State Security Service in the MUP structure speaks for itself, and it's not logical for them to give their operative documents to us because they are an institution at a certain level of competence. For us, at those meetings, in a way - I won't say that it was a position - but to a large extent it meant that the information was checked, reliable, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And as it was presented to you at these daily meetings, did you personally look at MUP documents or SDB documents, or were you simply told by other people at the meeting what their contents actually were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I said that before. These documents, this information, was something that I could see in the hands of my superior, but I didn't have it in my possession. And we were not informed about this directly. We would receive that based on reports indirectly and then find out about it through instructions, directives, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. The other source that you -- I'm sorry, I just have to go into some level of detail about a couple of these matters before I go to the main questions. The other source that you mentioned was material that came from the 1st Corps. And do you say the same thing about that material; namely, that you personally weren't shown those documents but you saw those documents in the hands of your superiors at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: If we're talking about information, it would happen that I wouldn't see this information. I could see it in somebody else's hands, but I wouldn't read it personally. When there was a report or a dispatch or something of a different nature that was less important or possibly if it affected my area of operational responsibility, then I would get documents of the type that we saw a little bit before, the document that I was shown a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to ask you a couple of questions about the 9th Brigade and then the 10th Brigade and their structures. You personally -- were you personally acquainted with Mr. Tomo Juric, the SVB representative at the 9th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I was acquainted with him that time when we had that one-day seminar. We sat together for two or three hours at the seminar, where we tried to provide them with instructions on work. He introduced himself to me. I even heard about him from before the war, but I had never met him personally until that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- and he was a person who, so far as you knew about his reputation, had a very good reputation as a professional policeman; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also -- you also mentioned the attendance of Ramiz Delalic, Celo, at a seminar. And I wanted to ask you this question -- well, perhaps I'll ask you a more general question first and then I'll come to Ramiz and the seminar in a minute. First of all, is it the fact that the rule on military security was introduced first in -- on the 9th of -- sorry, on the 11th of September, back in 1992, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And to your recollection, did persons of experience such as yourself, try to educate the volunteer and very new army that was defending Bosnia in those rules after the time when those rules were introduced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: These were not volunteers when the security service is concerned. There were certain procedures to admit people into the security and safety services. And I am sure that on the 11th of September, 1992 we adopted rules or instructions on the work of the security services which came down from the president and then it went into force, and it specified certain rules of conduct, measures, norms, our competencies, authorities, and so on. And as far as I know, all members of the services were informed about these rules, and it could not be applied outside of the security services because there were -- and this was something that was supposed to be confidential to the service because there was certain methods of work that should not be disclosed to the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, and I'm grateful for the explanation. What I wanted to ask you about, though, was this: In general terms, in that first year of the war were there a number of persons commanding units, even quite large units, who didn't have any formal military training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in such circumstances, how was it that the army explained to these commanders what the role of the SVB was, what its functions were, how they should deal with it, and questions of that nature? How were they educated about the role of the SVB in short?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't participate in meetings like that, and I was never provided any explanations to that effect. I can provide my own opinion, but that would be irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it wouldn't be irrelevant because you were there when the bombs were falling, so we'd be very grateful if you could just explain, just briefly, but explain how was it that the -- that the military security organ, the SVB, was brought to -- I suppose to put it bluntly, was brought into reality within these units which had untrained commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Did I understand you properly? The SVB, the military security service, or the SDB, State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military security service.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Let me first say that at the time there was a lot of fluctuation in the security services' staff, which was not good, in my opinion. But the nature of the work was such that we had to work fast and we had to find any possible way to resist or put up resistance against the aggressor. That's why we put together short seminars which we -- which were given by people of experience; although, of course, we were short of such staff. We had one seminar at the Bosna Hotel in early 1993. All members of the military security administration took part in this seminar, as well as members of the security service of the 1st Corps. And this, I think, was coordinated with people from the SDB at the time. The intention was to link these two services in a way so that people could get to know one another and also that they could coordinate and cooperate with a greater degree of confidence for one purpose. The purpose was the protection of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And bearing in mind that explanation, now, when Ramiz Delalic came to a seminar, was part of the purpose of that seminar to enable him and others in his position to work with the SVB in a proper way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No. It was like this: This was a completely different seminar where we went to the command of the 9th Motorised Brigade. As far as I can recall, this was in the first half of 1993, following an incident, quote unquote, a small problem that occurred when Ramiz Delalic found out that somebody was writing something about him behind his back. And after that -- after that, the chief of the military security administration tried to smooth these relations and in a way to improve the relationship between Ramiz Delalic and the security service. The two of us, I think, went to see Tomo Juric, the security chief of the brigade, who assembled all of the security service staff from that brigade. We went to the headquarters of the brigade. Ramiz Delalic wasn't there. He arrived at some point after a certain amount of time. He didn't interfere in our work. His conduct was very proper. He welcomed us. He thanked us for coming, for the instructions we were giving, and we didn't have any problems. I can't remember, but I think we even had coffee with him. And he said at the time that he had some information, something like that, that he wasn't really a persona who was welcome. He felt that he wanted to be in touch with us. He wanted to have good relations with us and contacts with us. And this is what he told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And I think you've indicated that took place before the incidents of the 2nd and 3rd of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Before. But I cannot tell you specifically when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. All right. Well, now -- I was asking you some questions about the 9th Brigade. And generally speaking, is -- is it fair to say the 9th Brigade fought on an important part of the front line and, to your knowledge, fought very well on that part of the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I think that it did fight at a very important place. It had an important task, and it was the largest section of the front line held by a single brigade in Sarajevo. It was thought of as a very strong brigade, even -- very well organised even, consisting of five battalions, which were all carrying out their tasks and performing in a satisfactory way. Although my opinion on this matter is not that relevant because I wasn't involved in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. And it was located, I think you indicated, fairly close to the old town, Stari Grad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The brigade, I think, also held a part of Stari Grad, if we're talking about the defence lines. I think that its right flank also held a part of Stari Grad, and for the most part it covered the municipality of Centar. Part of the brigade's command were in the old town, Stari Grad. There were also some commands in the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And concerning the 10th Brigade, did their area of defence also include part of the old town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The 10th Brigade, too, covered a part of the centre, Centar, and a part of the old town, Stari Grad, although I'm really not very well informed about that because I wasn't involved in that. I didn't live in those parts of town, so I'm not familiar well that. I know that it was a smaller brigade and that it consisted of mostly local inhabitants, people who lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to turn to the incidents of the 2nd of July. Is it the case that personnel from the SVB, military security, arrested a man named Senad Pezar who was an officer from the 10th Brigade on or about the 2nd of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I know that this happened, that this incident happened, but I cannot tell you specifically whether this happened before or after. I do think that it was before then, though. I wasn't really involved in that, so I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Well, I was going to put a line of questions to you about that, but I'll just ask you a couple. To your knowledge, was Senad Pezar arrested just before that trouble took place on the 2nd and 3rd of July and was he held for about a day, approximately a day, and then let go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It's possible. But as I said, I didn't take part in that, so I'm really not familiar with the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's okay. I just -- I really want to get the narrative right at the moment about that. Now, to your recollection, is it the case that following the incidents of the 2nd of July and the 3rd of July that the leaders of the 9th Brigade and the 10th Brigade made some requests of the Presidency; namely, that Fikret Muslimovic be removed from the leadership of the SVB and that the commander of the 1st Corps, a man with the nickname of Talijan, be replaced? Do you recall whether those requests or requirements were made by Ramiz Delalic and Musan Topalovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I can give you a reply like this: I think in the statement, when Ramiz Delalic was providing his statement, I think that that's what he told me. I cannot recall all the details, but I know that after those events Fikret Muslimovic was replaced. Also it's possible that the late Talijan was also replaced, although I'm not quite sure about the specific time. I know that they were replaced from those duties. I didn't know that this was because of that, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. And could I just ask you to be very -- and I'm not criticising you in any way. Could I just ask you to be careful to refer to your own knowledge. I'm certainly not asking you anything arising from the statements that other people have made but just from what you know. And I think you've indicated, is it accurate to say, that from your own knowledge you can't say what demands were made? Is that accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I didn't know personally, but I found this out when I was taking the statement from Ramiz Delalic, so I found out about it indirectly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I won't ask for your -- I won't ask for indirect evidence about that, and thank you for indicating it. Very well. Well, I'll move from that episode onwards. It's the fact that from the time of that -- during that confrontation on the 2nd and the 3rd, whatever the reasons for it may be, it's the fact that some civilian police were disarmed and some military security officers were also disarmed by units of the 9th and 10th Brigades; is that the fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can I ask you whether the name "Trebevic" or "Operation Trebevic" was conceived at that time or whether that came about at a later time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The Trebevic action was devised later, conceived later, and at that time nothing was said about it. There was no mention of it, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I refer you to a meeting of the constitution -- the Council for the Protection of Constitutional Order towards the end of July of 1993, about which this Tribunal has heard some evidence from another witness. Do you recall whether the operation designed to bring the 9th and 10th Brigades back into the line of control and command was commenced after that particular constitutional council meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I must say it's been a long day. Well, do you know the -- the council meeting that I'm referring to, the meeting of the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I did hear of that meeting and we talked about it earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I said what I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But to your knowledge, it's after that meeting that a plan developed for dealing with the 9th and 10th Brigades and their leadership; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware though that information-gathering and the collection of operative information was stepped up and intensified after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: After that meeting - I can't tell you the exact date - we received the view or the position of our superior to intensify our activities in relation to those brigades, to gather more information with a view to putting an end to those activities. But it wasn't specified when this would happen. No plan existed. And no names were given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just two final questions before I finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'll be finished with that topic, if the Court will just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, at that time, there was -- well, you've -- sorry, perhaps I'll turn it into one question. You indicated in answers to my learned friend Mr. Re that there was information that Sefer Halilovic was in touch with these two brigades. And I want to ask you this question: Bearing that in mind, I take it that the information that was gathered about those brigades was not shared, certainly not shared by you, but not shared by the SVB generally with Mr. Halilovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Within my competency -- competencies, within my scope of authorities, I did not have a right to do so, and also in accordance with the Rules of Service, it was not allowed to disclose such information. Perhaps only chief of the service or the commander superior to Mr. Halilovic could have done that, but I don't know whether that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I'm afraid that you have to stay here for the -- for the further testimony tomorrow. So during your stay in The Hague, do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I'll see you tomorrow morning. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
